claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed, unaltered oxide/passive film.
The stability and thickness of the native oxide/passive film are influenced by solution composition and temperature.
Increasing acidity, chloride concentration, and temperature destabilizes the native oxide/passive layer on Q235 steel.
Destabilization of the passive layer initiates localized corrosion breakdown.
Milder environments and lower temperatures preserve the passive film and delay corrosion onset.
Elevated temperature and increased chloride activity act synergistically to promote oxide breakdown and pitting initiation.
Breakdown of the oxide film reduces the overall corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
A destabilized oxide film accelerates anodic dissolution in harsh environments.
At temperatures of at least 100 °C and high chloride concentration, charge-transfer resistance will be approximately 25–50% lower than in the mild-temperature, low-chloride reference.
At temperatures of at least 100 °C and high chloride concentration, the weight-loss corrosion rate may double or more relative to the reference.
Untreated Q235 steel in near-neutral, low-chloride solution at 25 °C displays more stable passivation.
Untreated Q235 steel in near-neutral, low-chloride solution at 25 °C has lower mass-loss rates than steel in the proposed harsher environments.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy is applicable to evaluating corrosion resistance in a chloride solution.
Polarization curves are applicable to evaluating corrosion resistance in a chloride solution.
EIS can specifically determine passive-film stability and corrosion kinetics in uncoated Q235 steel.
Additional inhibitive species can alter the proposed passivation-breakdown mechanism.
Different steel compositions or protective coatings can change the corrosion-response mechanism.
Failure to observe a systematic corrosion-rate increase or polarization-resistance decrease as temperature or chloride concentration rises would falsify the proposed hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial material is defined as pre-exposure/as-received Q235, but the falsification design calls the coupons 'pre-exposed,' implying prior environmental exposure rather than an unexposed starting state.

The conditions state that pH around 1–4 is held constant across comparison groups, whereas the baseline is near-neutral. If that baseline is the reference used for the predicted comparison, pH is not held constant and the effects of temperature and chloride are confounded with acidity.
